title: The children Italy did not recognise
subtitle: Italian colonial laws of 1937 and 1940 banned conjugal-type relationships with Africans and barred fathers from recognising their mixed-race children. Nobody knows how many there were.

keyPoints.text: A 1937 decree-law banned 'conjugal' relationships between Italians and subjects of Italian East Africa; a 1940 law barred Italian fathers from recognising mixed-race children.
After the Ethiopian war the Italian population in the colony rose from under 5,000 to about 75,000, 78 percent of them men.
Estimates of the number of mixed-descent children differ: about 15,000 in one report, at least 20,000 in a journalist's count.

items.text: A decree-law of 19 April bans relationships 'of a conjugal nature' between Italian citizens and subjects of Italian East Africa; it is converted into law 2590 of 30 December.
A law of 29 June makes the birth of an Italo-Eritrean child an explicit clue to the offence.
Law 822 on 'rules concerning meticci' is passed; it bars the Italian father from recognising his mixed-race child.
The law is repealed in Italy by a legislative decree of 3 August.
The British administration in Eritrea repeals the Italian law by proclamation.

parts.text: The parliamentary report that gives these dates calls the 1940 law 'sciagurate', or wretched.
It also notes serious doubts about whether the 1947 decree is in force today.

blocks.prompt: Think first: why might nobody know the exact number?

parts.text: The report to parliament itself says that precise statistics do not exist, and its own estimates cite no source.

blocks.title: Estimates of mixed-descent children
blocks.sub: Three figures from two sources; they are not measurements

rows.label: Parliamentary report, born under the 1940 law, probably about

blocks.note: Figures as stated by the two sources: the journalist Vittorio Longhi in Internazionale (2021), and the report to the Italian parliament. Neither cites a study, and the periods are not the same.

parts.text: Of the 20,000 or more, the journalist says only five or six thousand were recognised.
The two estimates cannot be reconciled with the sources we have.
The report says the 1940 law stayed in force through most of the period when Italo-Eritrean children were born.
Most of these children grew up in Africa, so they do not explain ancestry in Italy itself.

blocks.title: A gap we cannot fill yet

parts.text: We have no account from the children themselves or their descendants. A counted list by a priest in Massawa names 349 people, a separate and much smaller figure.

gaps: The two estimates (about 15,000 and at least 20,000) cannot be reconciled; neither cites a study. Work by historians such as Barrera and Campassi is the next source to read.
No account from mixed-descent people or their families is quoted.
The legal status of the 1947 repeal decree is unclear in the report and is not covered here.
No one from Eritrea or Ethiopia has read this page yet.
